title: How Tacos Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of the taco, drawing heavily on Jeffrey Pilcher's book Planet Taco and Dave Ruse's research. They cover the tortilla's ancient origins in Mesoamerica and nixtamalization, the nutritional benefits of corn plus beans (complete protein), early Spanish-era tortilla use, the 19th-century origin of the word "taco" (mining explosive plugs, steam tacos, a Mexican dictionary entry), the rise of street tacos in Mexico City, the Lebanese-influenced tacos al pastor in Puebla, the Americanization of tacos in 1940s-50s Los Angeles (Taco House, Glenn Bell, Meat Like Cafe tacos dorados, hard shells), and the founding of Taco Bell in Downey, California in 1962 and the relocation of Taco Bell Numero Uno. The episode closes with hosts' favorite taco places and a listener mail about using the show to fall asleep.

entities.name: Planet Taco: A Global History of Mexican Food
Taco USA: How Mexican Food Conquered America

segments.title: Opening banter and Dave Ruse's taco research
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck talk about eating tacos, favorite taco delivery options, and how Dave Ruse came to research the episode after living in Mexico. They frame the question of how authentic Mexican tacos became the Americanized hard-shell version.

segments.title: Golden age of tacos and regional favorites
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the spread of good tacos across American cities and small towns, Old El Paso kit tacos, and personal favorites such as beef tongue, kabeza, carne asada, fish and shrimp tacos, and Korean barbecue tacos associated with Roy Choi.

segments.title: Ancient tortillas, nixtamalization, and nutrition
segments.summary: The tortilla is described as very old, dating to the domestication of corn in southern Mexico about 7,000 to 8,000 years ago, with the Maya and Olmec-era people developing alkaline nixtamalization. The process increases nutrient availability and calcium, and corn combined with beans forms a complete protein. The Nahuatl origin of the word nixtamal is explained.

segments.title: Pre-taco tortilla use and the word taco
segments.summary: Mesoamericans used tortillas as utensils and wrappers rather than tacos as such, with Montezuma reportedly using tortillas as spoons. The hosts discuss the Spanish word taco, meaning a plug or wad used in musket barrels, and the rejected Nahuatl etymology. They present a theory that the food name came from mine workers' lunches in Real del Monte, where the explosive charges were also called tacos.

segments.title: Taco as food appears and Mexico City street tacos
segments.summary: The earliest print use of taco as a food is traced to a novel, Los Bandidos del Río Frío. Mexico City's population growth around 1910 led to tacherías and street taco vendors bringing regional influences together.

segments.title: Tacos al pastor and Lebanese influence
segments.summary: The hosts describe the origin of tacos al pastor in Puebla, traced to Lebanese immigrants who sold vertical-spit lamb, which Mexican cooks adapted using pork, adding grilled pineapple. Chuck and Josh share a story about a Lebanese restaurant in Toledo.

segments.title: Americanized tacos in 1940s and 1950s Los Angeles
segments.summary: Segregated mid-century Los Angeles is described, with Taco House as an early non-Mexican-targeted taco restaurant and other taco-named restaurants in white and Black neighborhoods. Ground beef became the central ingredient. Glenn Bell is credited with shell innovation, alongside Joseph Pampa's 1949 fryer patent application and Rosendo Maldonado's patent.

segments.title: Glenn Bell, Meat Like Cafe, and the founding of Taco Bell
segments.summary: Glenn Bell learned to fry tacos dorados at the Meat Like Cafe in San Bernardino from the Rodriguez family, combining it with McDonald's-inspired efficiency. He opened Taco Tia in 1951 and later the first Taco Bell in Downey, California in 1962. The hosts discuss Taco Bell Numero Uno's relocation to Irvine in 2015 and Taco Bell's absence in Mexico.
